title: Open Source Finance: Yield Opportunity Costs
subtitle: Angry Crowds, Theft By Friction, Money As Technology, Accidents Of History, Jamie Dimon Wants To Eat Your Lunch, Open Source Finance
body_html:
Angry Crowds

There is a group of people, typically on the political left, who allege unfairness within the financial system: banks, funds, and other sophisticated financial market participants have stacked the deck against the common man. Challenge one of these people for specifics, and you will likely be met with lofty, abstracted diatribe against “the system.” It is a great irony that these people are correct but do not know how. A testament to intuition, perhaps. Or maybe it’s just that obvious.

This is not about freezing rent, abolishing interest, or otherwise distorting free markets. This is about open source finance: allowing everyday people to maximize their financial assets the way institutions do.

Theft By Friction

Treasury yields sit around 4% today1. Large financial institutions, investment funds, corporates, and banks have the scale to mobilize their assets around this anchor. Lending and investment decisions are informed by the Fed’s rates and treasury yields. Meanwhile, ordinary people earn an average of .07%2 yield on checking accounts and 0.38% on savings. With $5.9T3 worth of checkable deposits and currency held by American households, a three-month treasury bill yielding 3.6%, and an assumed pass-through operating margin of .5%, we are looking at ~$179B in foregone yield annually.4

High-yield savings accounts present an incomplete alternative: they offer competitive rates, but cannot act as a payment instrument. This forces the financial lives of ordinary people to orbit low-yield bank accounts.

This is a market failure caused by a separation between the payment and yield layers.

Money As Technology

Money is many things, but it’s a technology first. Stablecoins represent a significant development in money-as-technology by collapsing the payment and yield layers into a single instrument that exists on interoperable, programmable, settlement lag-free rails.

There is a possible world wherein stablecoins are used to purchase groceries, transmit fiat to friends and family, settle debts, and broadly compete with commercial bank money for yield.

Why do we not live in that world?

Accidents of History

Applications of blockchain to finance break the arbitrary jurisdictional division between the SEC and CFTC. Securities legislation born out of the ‘29 crash and centered on New York’s public equity markets and Commodities regulation shaped in Chicago’s futures pits struggle to accommodate something like Ethereum, which cycled through plausible readings as a commodity, security, and utility.

While Europe developed the MiCA5 Framework- defining and clarifying rules around stablecoins, required exchanges to register, and implemented market manipulation laws- Gensler’s SEC attempted to lazily map existing securities laws to these technologies. “Regulation by enforcement” meant arbitrary and inconsistent treatment toward crypto. Firms seeking guidance were ignored.

It took until 2025, two years after Europe, for the U.S to pass federal legislation concerning crypto. The GENIUS Act6 was not a market structure bill, but defined payment stablecoins and prohibited their issuers from passing yield through to end-users.

Stablecoins as a high-yielding payment instrument available to ordinary Americans would seem dead on the spot after the passing of GENIUS. But there was a gap: non-issuers were not prevented from passing yield through to consumers. And so they did.

Enter CLARITY7. This market structure bill would broadly prohibit yield pass-through, but leave an intentional carve-out for stablecoin holders to receive “activity-based rewards.”

Jamie Dimon Wants To Eat Your Lunch

If it is the case that using stablecoins to purchase goods and services qualifies as “activity,” then CLARITY enables high-yield payment instruments. Incumbents have noticed this and raised concerns about consumer protection, decreases in available credit, and systemic risk of consumers migrating from commercial bank deposits to stablecoins. These arguments can be evaluated on their merits, and are not entirely unfounded. Stablecoin issuers do not have the same regulatory reporting, capitalization, and risk mitigation standards that large banks do. There are novel risk vectors associated with mass adoption of stablecoins. Issuers, custodians, smart contracts, and the host of other ecosystem components are novel and untested financial infrastructure.

But it takes a brief inspection of the incentives to see how much banks have to lose, and how much we have to gain. Licensed taxi drivers objected to rideshare apps, hotels resisted Airbnb, and banks are worried about stablecoins.

The American Bankers Association projects stablecoin total issuance to bloom from today’s $300B8 to $2T, and frames this growth as having the potential to reduce consumer, small-business, and agricultural lending by 20%9. It also notes the risk of small, regional banks being unable to replace retail deposits with wholesale funding, and failing. The resulting increase in concentration within the banking industry rings undesirable.

A broader view of these considerations must be taken. Depository institutions hold $3T10 in reserves with the Fed, and total US commercial deposits are $19T.11 At a $2T issuance, stablecoins would represent 10.5% of deposits. Not insignificant, but there is reason to believe lending capacity can absorb deposit flight or replacement on the margin.12 Jamie Dimon and others have resisted CLARITY because of the threat of surplus from high-yield payment instruments reallocating towards consumers.

Open Source Finance

The angry crowds are correct: the deck is stacked. Frictions of legacy infrastructure, regulatory capture, and incumbents working to determine the bounds of their own disruption work to keep that $179B in the hands of the few rather than the many. At the time of writing, the CLARITY Act has cleared the Senate Banking Committee and awaits a floor vote. The ABA’s projected $1.7T growth in stablecoin issuance represents depositor upside, the potential for consumers to live in that possible world where high-yielding payment instruments capture value previously funneled to large institutions. Whether ordinary Americans get to live in that possible world will be decided shortly.
